'''Carolyn Eisele''' (June 13, 1902 – January 15, 2000) was an American [[mathematician]] and [[history of mathematics|historian of mathematics]] known as an expert on the works of [[Charles Sanders Peirce]].<ref name="hm">{{citation
 | last = Ketner | first = Kenneth Laine
 | doi = 10.1016/0315-0860(82)90126-4
 | issue = 3
 | journal = [[Historia Mathematica]]
 | mr = 667604
 | pages = 326–332
 | title = Carolyn Eisele's place in Peirce studies
 | volume = 9
 | year = 1982| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref><ref name="tcsps">{{citation
 | last = Ketner | first = Kenneth Laine
 | issue = 4
 | journal = Transactions of the Charles S. Peirce Society
 | jstor = 40320857
 | pages = 475–489
 | title = Carolyn Eisele (1902–2000)
 | volume = 37
 | year = 2001}}.</ref><ref name="isis">{{citation
 | last1 = Gleason | first1 = Mary Louise
 | last2 = Dauben | first2 = Joseph W. |author2-link=Joseph Dauben
 | doi = 10.1086/430655
 | issue = 4
 | journal = [[Isis (journal)|Isis]]
 | mr = 2147011
 | pages = 649–652
 | title = Carolyn Eisele, 1902–2000
 | volume = 95
 | year = 2004| s2cid = 145676773
 }}</ref><ref name="iupui">{{citation|title=Carolyn Eisele Collection|url=http://liberalarts.iupui.edu/iat/index.php/centers/carolyn_eisele_collection|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304055951/http://liberalarts.iupui.edu/iat/index.php/centers/carolyn_eisele_collection|publisher=Institute for American Thought, Indiana University–Purdue University Indianapolis|access-date=2014-08-03|archive-date=4 March 2016}}.</ref>

== Education and career ==
Eisele was born on June 13, 1902, in [[The Bronx]], [[New York City]].<ref name="isis" />
She studied at [[Hunter College High School]] and then [[Hunter College]], graduating [[Phi Beta Kappa]] in 1923.<ref name="tcsps" /><ref name="isis" />
She earned a master's degree in mathematics and education from [[Columbia University]] in 1925.<ref name="tcsps" /><ref name="isis" />
At that time, Columbia did not offer Ph.D.s in mathematics to women, but Eisele continued her graduate studies at the [[University of Chicago]] (where she studied [[differential geometry]]) and the [[University of Southern California]] before returning home to New York, without a doctorate, to care for her heavily injured father.<ref name="isis" /> Her studies also included [[opera]] singing, with  Jeanne Fourestier in Paris in 1931 and later with Los Angeles-based voice coach Morris Halpern, whom she married in 1943.<ref name="isis" />

Eisele taught mathematics at [[Hunter College]] for nearly 50 years.<ref name="isis" /><ref name="iupui" /> She began teaching as an instructor there after her college graduation in 1923,<ref name="hm" /><ref name="tcsps" /><ref name="isis" /> eventually reached the rank of full professor in 1965,<ref name="hm" /><ref name="tcsps" /> and retired in 1972.<ref name="isis" /><ref name="tcsps" />

Eisele died on January 15, 2000<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/01/16/classified/paid-notice-deaths-eisele-carolyn.html|title=Paid Notice: Deaths EISELE, CAROLYN|date=2000-01-16|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-06-13|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> in [[Manhattan]], New York City.<ref name="isis" />

== Peirce studies ==
As a student at Columbia University, Eisele took a course in the [[history of mathematics]] from [[David Eugene Smith]], but her professional contributions to the subject began in 1947, when she took a sabbatical to prepare for a course in the history of mathematics that she had been asked to teach at Hunter College.<ref name="isis" /> While working in the [[George Arthur Plimpton]] collection at the Columbia University library, she found a manuscript by [[Charles Sanders Peirce]] on [[Fibonacci]]'s ''[[Liber Abaci]]'' and in 1951 she published a paper about her discovery in ''[[Scripta Mathematica]]''.<ref name="tcsps" /><ref name="isis" /> Other early works of Eisele on Peirce included his correspondence with [[Simon Newcomb]] and his [[Peirce quincuncial projection]] for maps of the world.<ref name="isis" /> Her work on Peirce took a holistic view, in which his contributions to philosophy and logic were treated as part of a whole together with his contributions to mathematics and science, rather than as separate and unrelated chapters in his life.<ref name="hm" />

Eisele served as the president of the Charles S. Peirce Society from 1973 to 1975.<ref name="isis" /><ref name="iupui" />
In 1976, Eisele began publishing a multi-volume collection of Peirce's writings that she had edited, the ''New Elements of Mathematics'', and in the same year she helped organize the Peirce Bicentennial International Congress in Amsterdam.<ref name="hm" /><ref name="tcsps" /><ref name="isis" />

== Books ==
*''Studies in the Science and Mathematical Philosophy of Charles S. Peirce: Essays by Carolyn Eisele'' (1979)<ref name="isis" /><ref name="iupui" />
*''Historical Perspectives on Peirce’s Logic of Science: A History of Science'' (1985)<ref name="tcsps" /><ref name="iupui" />

== Awards and honors ==
Eisele was named a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 1960.<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.aaas.org/fellows/historic|title=Historic Fellows|publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science|access-date=2021-04-15}}</ref>

On her retirement from Hunter College in 1972, Eisele joined the Hunter Hall of Fame.<ref name="isis" /> She was given honorary doctorates from [[Texas Tech University]] in 1980 and from [[Lehigh University]] in 1982.<ref name="hm" /><ref name="tcsps" /><ref name="isis" /><ref name="iupui" />

In 1980, Eisele became an honorary member of the crew of the [[United States Coast Guard]] ship ''USC&GSS Peirce''.<ref name="isis" /> In 1981, a symposium on Peirce studies was held in her honor at Hunter College, the proceedings of which were published as a [[festschrift]] in ''[[Historia Mathematica]]''.<ref name="hm" /><ref name="isis" /> In 1985, Eisele was given the Behavioral Sciences, History and Philosophy of Sciences award from the [[New York Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="dictionary">"[https://www.oxfordreference.com/abstract/10.1093/acref/9780199754663.001.0001/acref-9780199754663-e-287?rskey=Nk5IcR&result=1 Eisele, Carolyn (1902–2000)]." In John R. Shook and Richard T. Hull, eds. ''[[The Dictionary of Modern American Philosophers|Dictionary of Modern American Philosophers]]''. Bristol: Thoemmes, 2005. p.715.</ref> Her other honors include a Doctor of Humanities degree awarded by [[Texas Tech University]] in 1980 and a Doctor of Science degree awarded in 1982 by [[Lehigh University]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kaufman|first1=Authur|last2=Dauben|first2=Joseph|last3=Gleason|first3=Mary Louise|date=2001|title=Carolyn Eisele, 1902-2000|journal=Proceedings and Addresses of the American Philosophical Association|volume=74|issue=5|pages=228–229|issn=0065-972X|jstor=3218596}}</ref>
